title: The Winery
description: Fermentation, extraction, oak and time: the steps that turn the same fruit into very different wines.
L: Explain how temperature changes a fermentation

Fermentation is yeast turning sugar into alcohol, carbon dioxide and heat. The winemaker's main tool is temperature. Cool fermentations, 12 to 18 degrees Celsius, keep fresh, fruity aromas in whites. Warmer ones, 25 to 32, extract colour and tannin in reds. Above about 35 degrees, yeast can die and fermentation may stop.
Temperature is the winemaker's main dial

Wild or ambient yeasts live on grapes and in the winery. Many winemakers rely on them, saying they add complexity, but they are less predictable. Cultured yeasts are selected strains, chosen for reliability, speed or particular aromas. Either way, the dominant species is Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
Ambient for complexity, cultured for control
Why are most white wines fermented cool?
Low temperatures keep delicate aromas. Warmer fermentations suit reds, which need colour and tannin.

Stainless steel is inert and easy to cool, keeping pure fruit. Concrete holds a stable temperature and allows a little air. Oak barrels add flavour and let small amounts of oxygen in. Clay vessels, like amphorae or Georgian qvevri, are ancient and returning to fashion.
Match each vessel to its main effect.
The vessel shapes texture and flavour as much as the yeast does.
Temperature controls the speed and style of fermentation
Ambient yeasts add complexity; cultured yeasts add reliability
Steel, concrete, oak and clay each shape the wine differently
Describe the steps of white winemaking
Explain skin contact and its effect

White grapes are crushed and pressed, usually soon after picking. The juice settles to drop solids, then ferments cool, often in stainless steel. The new wine may rest on its lees, then is clarified, stabilised and bottled. Many aromatic whites are bottled within months to keep them fresh.
Press, settle, ferment cool, clarify, bottle

Juice browns quickly in air, like a cut apple, and loses fruit. Winemakers use cold, inert gases like carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide to protect it. Some leave skins and juice together for a few hours before pressing, called skin contact, to draw out aroma, but too long adds bitterness and colour.
Cold, inert gas and sulphur protect the juice
Put the steps of making a white wine in order.
White wines are pressed before fermentation, unlike reds.

Ferment white grapes on their skins, like a red, for days or months, and you get an orange or amber wine. It has tannin, deeper colour and flavours of dried fruit, tea and nuts. The method is ancient in Georgia and returned in Friuli and elsewhere from the 1990s.
White grapes, red method, orange wine
In white winemaking, the grapes are usually pressed before fermentation.
Yes. For whites, the juice is separated from the skins first. Reds are pressed after fermentation, because skin contact is needed for colour and tannin.
White grapes are pressed first, then the juice ferments cool
Cold, inert gas and sulphur keep the juice fresh
Long skin contact turns white grapes into orange wine
Describe the steps of red winemaking
Explain the ways to extract colour and tannin

Black grapes are destemmed and crushed. Juice, skins and seeds ferment together, often at 25 to 30 degrees. The skins float to the top and form a cap. After fermentation the wine may stay on the skins to extract more, then is pressed. The free-run wine and the press wine are kept separate.

The cap of skins must be kept in contact with the juice to extract colour and tannin and to stop it drying out and spoiling. Punching down pushes the cap under. Pumping over sprays juice from the bottom over the top. Rack and return drains the tank and pours the juice back. Each gives a different intensity of extraction.
Punch down, pump over, rack and return
Why must the cap of skins be managed during red fermentation?
To extract colour and tannin and avoid spoilage
A floating cap dries out and can spoil. Keeping it wet extracts colour, tannin and flavour.

In carbonic maceration, whole bunches go into a tank filled with carbon dioxide. Fermentation starts inside each berry, without yeast at first. This gives soft, low-tannin reds with bright aromas of banana, bubblegum and cherry. It is the classic method of Beaujolais, where many wines use a partial version.
Whole berries, CO2, fruity soft reds
Which are ways to extract colour and tannin from the cap?
Cold settling is used to clear white juice, not to manage a red cap.
Reds ferment with their skins, then are pressed
Punching down, pumping over and rack and return manage extraction
Carbonic maceration gives soft, fruity reds like Beaujolais

Most rosé is made from black grapes with skin contact of a few hours, then the juice is run off and fermented cool like a white. Direct pressing gives the palest colour, with juice just touched by the skins during the press. Longer maceration gives deeper colour and more fruit.
Hours of contact, then made like a white

Rosé colour depends on grape, contact time and temperature. Thin-skinned Grenache gives pale pink quickly; thick-skinned Syrah colours fast. Provence's pale rosés, many with less than 6 hours of contact, now set the market fashion, so producers plan colour as carefully as flavour.
Grape and contact time set the colour
The rosé method that draws juice off a red wine tank is called ____.
Saignée means bleeding. Pigeage and remontage are cap management methods for reds; dosage belongs to sparkling wine.

In the EU, mixing red and white wine to make still rosé is not allowed. Champagne is the exception: most rosé Champagne is made by adding a small amount of still red wine to the white base. Outside Europe, blending is allowed in many countries.
Blending is banned for most EU still rosé
Which wine can legally be made by blending red and white wine in the EU?
Rosé Champagne is the exception. Still rosé in the EU must be made from skin contact or saignée.
Most rosé is made with a short skin contact, then fermented like a white
Grape and contact time set the colour
Blending red and white is banned for EU still rosé, except Champagne
Explain what oak adds to wine
Compare new and old, French and American oak
Name the cheaper alternatives to barrels

Oak does two things. It adds flavour: vanilla, toast, clove, smoke and coconut. And, in barrels, it lets a little oxygen in slowly, which softens tannins and helps the wine develop. Small barrels, like the 225-litre Bordeaux barrique, have more effect than large casks.
New or old, French or American

New barrels give the most flavour; after three or four uses they add little but still allow oxygen. Toasting the inside over fire changes flavours from vanilla to smoke. French oak, Quercus petraea and robur, gives subtle spice and fine tannin. American oak, Quercus alba, gives stronger vanilla and coconut, typical of traditional Rioja.
Match each oak choice to its effect.
The age, origin and toast of a barrel decide what it adds.

Barrels are expensive, around 1,000 euros each for French oak. For wines at lower prices, winemakers add oak chips or staves to a steel tank. They give oak flavour quickly but not the slow oxygen of a barrel. Micro-oxygenation can supply that separately.
Chips and staves: flavour without the barrel
Oak chips give a wine both oak flavour and the slow oxygen exchange of a barrel.
Not true. Chips and staves add flavour, but in a sealed steel tank there's no slow oxygen through the wood. That's why barrels remain prized.
Oak adds flavour and, in barrels, slow oxygen
New, small, toasted barrels add the most
Chips and staves are cheaper and add flavour only

Reductive maturation keeps oxygen out, in steel tanks or full vessels, preserving fresh, primary fruit. Oxidative maturation lets some air in, in barrels or partly filled vessels, which softens tannin and adds notes of nut, caramel and dried fruit. Most wines sit between the two.

Blending combines wines to make a better whole. Grapes add different qualities: Cabernet for structure, Merlot for fruit. Plots add different notes. Vintages, in Champagne or Port, give consistency. Vessels, oak and steel, bring balance. A good blend is more than the sum of its parts.
Blend grapes, plots, vintages or vessels
Which of these are common reasons to blend?
To keep a house style consistent across years
To make every wine identical worldwide
To raise the legal alcohol limit
Blending balances grapes, plots and vessels, and blending vintages keeps a house style steady, as in Champagne. It has nothing to do with legal limits or global uniformity.

Once bottled, a wine keeps changing slowly. Fruit fades, tannins soften and tertiary notes like leather, earth and honey develop. Only some wines gain from it, mainly those with high acidity, tannin or sugar and plenty of concentration. Some regions require bottle ageing before release, as Rioja Gran Reserva does.
Bottle age softens and adds complexity
Which wine is most likely to improve with ten years in bottle?
A concentrated, tannic red from a top vineyard
Long ageing needs concentration and structure, like tannin and acidity. Light, fruity wines are made to drink young.
Reductive maturation keeps fruit fresh; oxidative adds development
Blending combines grapes, plots, vintages or vessels for balance
Only structured, concentrated wines gain from long bottle age
Explain why wine is clarified and stabilised
Compare cork, screw cap and other closures
Explain the effect of the closure on ageing

Before bottling, wine is made clear and stable. Fining adds an agent like bentonite clay or egg white that binds haze-causing particles. Filtration strains them out. Cold stabilisation chills the wine to drop tartrate crystals, the harmless wine diamonds sometimes found in bottles. Some producers skip these steps, accepting a little haze.

Natural cork lets in tiny amounts of oxygen, but about 1 to 3% of bottles can be tainted by TCA, which smells of damp cardboard. Screw caps let in very little oxygen and cannot cause cork taint, so they keep fruit fresh; they are standard in New Zealand and Australia. Technical corks and glass stoppers sit in between.
Cork breathes a little; screw caps barely at all
What are the crystals sometimes found in a bottle of white wine?
Tartrates are natural salts of tartaric acid. They are harmless and show the wine wasn't cold stabilised.
A screw cap isn't a sign of a cheap wine. Many top Rieslings, Sauvignon Blancs and even fine reds use them to keep the wine exactly as the winemaker intended.
Wines sealed with screw caps cannot suffer from cork taint.
Yes. TCA, the cause of cork taint, comes from natural cork. Screw caps avoid it, although other faults are still possible.
Fining, filtration and cold stabilisation make wine clear and stable
Corks let in a little oxygen but risk TCA
Screw caps keep wine fresh and avoid cork taint
Explain how whites, reds and rosés are made
Describe the effects of oak and maturation
Explain the final steps before bottling
Put the steps of making a red wine in order.
Reds ferment with skins first and are pressed afterwards.
Match each technique to its result.
Each method creates a different style from the same fruit.
What does a new oak barrel add that oak chips do not?
Chips can add flavour, but only barrels let oxygen in slowly through the wood.
Most white wines ferment at warmer temperatures than reds.
Not true. Whites ferment cool to keep aromas; reds ferment warmer to extract colour and tannin.
Which steps prepare a wine for bottling?
Punching down is part of red fermentation, not the bottling stage.
Whites are pressed before fermentation; reds after
Rosé is made with short skin contact; blending is rare in Europe
Oak and maturation add flavour, oxygen and complexity
Fining, filtering and closures prepare and protect the wine
